parts.name: the wrong entry (APC into Alexa Fluor 700)

runs.reply:
The wrong value is the APC-A into Alexa Fluor 700-A spillover. The matrix in the files (the $SPILLOVER keyword of D01_Unstim) has 10.98%, and the single-stain controls give 15.8%. That leaves APC under-compensated by about 4.8 points.

The check covered all 14 single-stain controls. The only other flagged entry is BV605-A into BV650-A, which is 18.39% against a suggested 18.18%. That difference is small enough to be normal noise.

BV510-A (the viability stain) was also flagged, because its positive cells are brighter in several detectors at once. That points to autofluorescence in the heat-killed cells, not to a spillover error, so I left it alone.

Stimulation raises the percentage of CD25+ cells among CD4 T cells, from a mean of 7.6% unstimulated to 34.5% stimulated.

**Gating.** I added two gates under the existing T cells gate. The first is CD4 T (CD4 ≥ 5000, CD8 ≤ 2000). The second is CD25+ (CD25 ≥ 1800 on PE-A). I set both cutoffs by eye from the plots of donor D01, and they apply to every sample. Both gates are still proposals for you to accept or reject.

**Test.** The design is paired, with the same six donors measured in both conditions. The paired t-test gives p = 5.0e-9 (mean difference −26.9 percentage points, 95% CI −27.8 to −26.1, comparing unstimulated with stimulated). The exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test gives p = 0.031, the smallest p-value possible with six pairs. All six donors rose, from 5–11% unstimulated to 32–37% stimulated.

I report the paired t-test p-value because the paired differences are very consistent across donors. I did not run the robustness check on the gate positions, so I can't say how much the exact percentages depend on the CD25 cutoff. The direction is unambiguous either way.

ANSWER: {"direction": "up", "p": 4.98e-9}

Stimulation raises the percentage of CD25+ cells among CD4 T cells, from about 9.8% to about 37.8%.

- **Gating:** I added a CD4 T gate under the existing T cells (CD4 above 4000 and CD8 below 3000 on the compensated, scaled axes). Under it I split CD25 at 1500 on PE-A. That threshold sits at the valley between the CD25-dim and CD25-bright populations in the plots I checked (D01 unstimulated and stimulated). I did not look at the other donors' plots or refine the gate per sample. Both gates are proposals waiting for your review.
- **Test:** The design is paired, with the same six donors measured unstimulated and stimulated, so I used a paired t-test on CD25+ as a percentage of CD4 T cells.
- **Result:** Every donor went up, from 7–14% unstimulated to 35–40% stimulated. The mean change is +28.1 points (95% CI 27.0 to 29.1), with a paired t-test p of 1.4e-8.
- **Rank test:** The exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test gives p = 0.031. With six pairs, that is the smallest p it can reach.

ANSWER: {"direction": "up", "p": 1.41775e-8}

I ran acquisition QC on all four samples (PeacoQC, flow rate, margin events and per-channel drift).

- **A01** is clean. It scored 100 with no findings.
- **A02** has a clog. The flow rate dropped at 8–11 s, which is what a partial clog looks like, and 7.5% of events were removed. The score was 82.
- **A03** has drift. Every fluorescence channel fell over the run: BV510 by 33%, BV605 by 40%, BV711 by 29% and BV786 by 38%. The flow rate was normal and almost no events were removed, so this is a gradual signal loss rather than an event-level problem. The score was 80.
- **A04** has an air bubble. There was a burst of events with a signal drop in FSC-H at 12–13 s, and 24% of events were removed. BV605 also drifted down by 23%, but that is probably a side effect of the bubble. The score was 44.

QC has only been proposed. I haven't added a QC gate to the gating tree.

ANSWER: {"A01": "clean", "A02": "clog", "A03": "drift", "A04": "bubble"}

parts.name: the cause (a degraded tandem)
parts.detail: Tandem dye degradation: PE-Cy7 in the donor samples has degraded more than in its single-stain control (light, heat or fixation damage to the Cy7 acceptor). It emits about 11.5% more as PE, so signal spills into the PE channel as a diagonal and the reference spectrum no longer matches.

answer.cause: Tandem dye degradation: PE-Cy7 in the donor samples has degraded more than in its single-stain control (light, heat or fixation damage to the Cy7 acceptor). It emits about 11.5% more as PE, so signal spills into the PE channel as a diagonal and the reference spectrum no longer matches.

runs.reply:
PE-Cy7 is the dye with the problem. In the unmixed donor samples it has degraded more than its single-stain control did.

- I unmixed the three donors with the 25 single-stain references and per-event autofluorescence.
- I ran the unmixing diagnosis on Donor_S1 only; I did not run it on Donor_S2 or Donor_S3.
- In Donor_S1, the PE channel's negative population rises in proportion to PE-Cy7 signal. The slope is 0.115 of PE per unit of PE-Cy7 (z ≈ 900).
- About 67% of the PE-Cy7-positive events sit on that line, compared with 0.01% on a flat one. Across PE-Cy7's range it moves PE by about 25 noise SDs.
- The donor's PE-Cy7 emits about 11.5% more as PE than the control's did. That is the pattern of the Cy7 acceptor breaking down and the PE donor emitting directly. Light, heat, fixation or age between staining the control and the sample would all cause it.
- The residual stays small (about 0.05) because the model absorbs the lost emission. The problem shows as a diagonal on a PE versus PE-Cy7 plot.
- The other tandem-leak checks (for example PE-Cy5→PE, BV650→BV421) showed no consensus, so they are not supported as problems.

The fix is to re-stain the PE-Cy7 control from the same vial at the same time as the samples. The alternative is the Diagnose tab's "Use the PE-Cy7 spectrum this sample shows", which swaps in a spectrum with 11.5% more PE emission. That change is yours to apply in the Spectral view. After that, unmix again.

ANSWER: {"dye": "PE-Cy7", "cause": "Tandem dye degradation: PE-Cy7 in the donor samples has degraded more than in its single-stain control (light, heat or fixation damage to the Cy7 acceptor). It emits about 11.5% more as PE, so signal spills into the PE channel as a diagonal and the reference spectrum no longer matches."}

runs.reply:
The dye is PE-Cy7. After unmixing the three donors, the diagnosis on Donor_S1 found one cause, with high confidence. I didn't run it on Donor_S2 or Donor_S3.

- **Evidence:** PE's negative population rises in proportion to PE-Cy7 brightness, at about 0.115 of PE per unit of PE-Cy7 (z ≈ 900). On a plot of the two channels this shows as a diagonal. 67.5% of the PE-Cy7-positive events lie on that line.
- **Cause:** In the donor samples, PE-Cy7 emits about 11.5% more of its light as PE than it did in its single-stain control. That is the signature of tandem dye degradation, where the acceptor's energy transfer breaks down and the PE donor emits directly. Light, heat, fixation or time since staining can all cause it.
- **Residual:** The residual is small (about 0.05) because the lost emission is the donor's, which the model holds. The problem therefore doesn't show up as a poor fit.
- **Fix:** Use a PE-Cy7 control stained from the same vial at the same time as the samples. Failing that, the Spectral view's Diagnose tab can replace the reference spectrum with the one the sample shows, which is PE-Cy7 plus 11.5% more PE emission. Then unmix again.

The same check also listed small leak values for BV650→BV421, PE-Cy5→PE and BUV563→BUV395, but none had consensus.

ANSWER: {"dye": "PE-Cy7", "cause": "Tandem dye degradation: PE-Cy7 in the donor samples has degraded more than in its single-stain control, so it emits extra light as PE (about 11.5%). The unmixing reference no longer matches, and PE-Cy7 spills into the PE channel."}

parts.name: the amount (125 ng: twice the amount near 90% of saturation)

runs.reply:
The tool recommends **125 ng per test**.

I ran the titration on the 10 stained CD4-PE tubes (1.953 to 1000 ng), using all events on the PE channel. I left out the unstained tube and the voltage-walk tubes. I didn't gate on lymphocytes first, because no gates exist in the workspace. The result is therefore for all events, not a lymphocyte gate.

- **Peak stain index:** The stain index peaks at 62.5 ng (310) and is almost the same at 31.25 ng (299) and 125 ng (308).
- **Saturation:** A saturation curve fitted to the stain index reaches 90% of saturation at about 39 ng.
- **Recommended amount:** The method picks the first tested amount at or above twice that, 78 ng, which is 125 ng.
- **Above 125 ng:** The negative population gets brighter and broader (negative rSD 31% at 125 ng, 69% at 1000 ng). The positive signal barely rises, so the stain index falls to 143 at 1000 ng.
- **Below 31 ng:** The stain index drops (266 at 15.63 ng), so the antibody is not yet saturating.

The percent positive stays flat at about 36–38% across the range. At 125 ng the stain index is within 1% of the maximum and the negatives are still tight. The 62.5 ng tube has the highest stain index, so it would also work if you want to save antibody.

ANSWER: {"amountNg": 125}

parts.name: the amount (125 ng: twice the amount near 90% of saturation)

runs.reply:
I analysed the titration on the PE channel (CD4) across all ten stained tubes, with all events as the population. I didn't gate lymphocytes first.

**Recommendation: 125 ng per test.**

- **Saturation:** a saturation curve fitted to the stain index reaches 90% of its maximum at about 39 ng.
- **Rule used:** the recommended amount is the first tested amount at or above twice the 90% point (about 78 ng). In your series that is 125 ng.
- **Peak resolution:** the stain index is highest at 62.5 ng (310). At 125 ng it is almost the same (308).
- **Excess antibody:** above 125 ng the positive signal stops rising, because the positive median is already near its plateau. The negative population gets brighter and broader instead. Its rSD goes from 31% at 125 ng to 69% at 1000 ng, and the stain index falls to 143 at 1000 ng.
- **Under-staining:** at 15.6 ng or less, the positive median and stain index are clearly lower.
- **Positive fraction:** the percent positive stays flat at about 36–38% across the whole series, so the choice doesn't depend on it.

ANSWER: {"amountNg": 125}

parts.name: the inactive compounds (CW-105; CW-106 either way)

runs.reply:
**CW-103 is the most potent inhibitor, with an IC50 of about 3.2 nM** (95% CI 2.8–3.6 nM, R² 0.997).

I measured CD69+ as a percentage of live T cells. I normalized it to the controls as % inhibition and fitted a four-parameter log-logistic curve for each compound. The plate quality is excellent (Z′ = 0.84).

| Compound | IC50 (nM) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| CW-103 | 3.2 | Most potent |
| CW-101 | 27 | CI 26–28, R² 0.9998 |
| CW-102 | 302 | CI 209–436 |
| CW-104 | about 1,270 | CI 559–2,885, shallow curve, R² 0.93 |
| CW-106 | about 17,800 | Beyond the highest dose of 10 µM, so the fit extrapolates (R² 0.76) |
| CW-105 | none | Flat curve (R² 0.13), no better than a flat line (p = 0.30) |

**CW-105 shows no inhibition at the doses tested.**

CW-106 is borderline. Its fit is statistically distinguishable from flat (p = 0.001), but the IC50 lies above the tested range. It gives only partial inhibition at the top dose, so I did not count it as inactive.

ANSWER: {"mostPotent": "CW-103", "ic50nM": 3.2, "inactive": ["CW-105"]}
